[0] everyday_reading (E): In everyday writing, quotes only mark words, "10" is the number ten, and two texts are 'equal' when they read the same. In Java a String is an object reached through a reference: "10" is text, + concatenates, and == compares references rather than contents.
[1] misconception (M) -> StringLiteralNoObject: wrong rule: a string literal isn't a String object until the constructor is called. Right rule: A string literal is already a String object, so "text".length() works directly.
[2] misconception (M) -> EqualsComparesReferences: wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.
[3] misconception (M) -> ArithmeticOnNumericStrings: wrong rule: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers. Right rule: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.
[4] inconsistent_trace (T) -> StringLiteralNoObject: Points to LT (String expressions produce references to String objects, and operations build new strings). Applied unevenly, a student compares with equals in one test and == in another, or treats "12" as a number in one + and as text in the next. (here mixing in: "a string literal isn't a String object until the constructor is called")
[5] misconception (M) -> StringIsPrimitive: wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).
[6] misconception (M) -> EqualityOperatorComparesObjectsValues: wrong rule: == compares contents (the String == bug). Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.
[7] misconception (M) -> StringRelationalComparison: wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.

[0] names_the_element (N): String: Java's built-in non-primitive (reference) type for a sequence of characters.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A String literal is characters in double quotes and denotes a String object. + concatenates. Contents are compared with equals, not ==. < and > are not defined for Strings, and Strings are immutable.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): A String expression is evaluated left to right. At each + with a String operand, the other operand is converted to a String and a new String object is made. Methods such as toUpperCase return a new String and leave the original unchanged.
[1] output_prediction (OP): "Hi, " + "Bob" is "Hi, Bob" and "1234" + "99" is "123499". s.equals(t) is true exactly when the characters match, while "abc" == "ab" + x can be false for x = "c".
[2] one_step_execution (OS): No operation changes an existing String. s = s + "x" makes s refer to a new String, and other variables still referring to the old one are unaffected.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): + produces a new String whenever at least one operand is a String; the other operand is converted to text first.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): 'a' is a char (one 16-bit character code, a primitive); "a" is a String (a sequence of characters, an object). 'a' + 'b' is the int 195, while "a" + "b" is "ab".
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Strings handle all text: messages, labels, formatted output and command-line arguments (args[] are Strings and must be parsed before arithmetic).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> StringLiteralNoObject: Replacing equals with == may still pass for two identical literals but fails for computed or input strings. Changing "5" to 5 turns concatenation into addition.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use String for any text: names, messages, tokens and output lines. Convert to int or double with Integer.parseInt or Double.parseDouble before arithmetic. Use char for a single character whose code matters.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: String contents are compared with equals; == compares references. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Comparing a String read from input or built by + against a literal with == or !=: false even though the text matches.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: < and > (and - * /) are defined only for primitive types, not for Strings. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: s < t, "10" - 1, "6" * "2": 'bad operand types for binary operator'.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A String variable can hold only a String (or null). Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: String message = 123;: 'incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String'.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A method cannot be called through a null reference. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Calling length(), equals() or charAt() on a String variable whose value is null: NullPointerException.
